Day first reads all three, wins the column, and 03/04/2025 becomes 3 April for every row.

A column holding only 03/04/2025 and 05/06/2025 reads fully both ways, and the data cannot break that tie. A convention from outside the data has to, such as the locale of the browser. The importer should report that it guessed, because a wrong guess produces dates that look valid.

The whole column reveals the separators

Countries write numbers differently. One thousand two hundred thirty-four and fifty-six hundredths is 1,234.56 in the US and 1.234,56 in Germany. The dot and the comma swap roles, and code written for one convention misreads the other.

Price columns from different systems hold 1.234,56, 1 234,56 with a non-breaking space, €1,234.56, and (250,00), which accounting software uses for a negative amount. parseFloat reads each of them from the left and stops at the first character it does not expect.

parseFloat("1.234,56");  // 1.234
parseFloat("1 234,56");  // 1
parseFloat("€1,234.56"); // NaN

A validator catches NaN. 1.234 passes the same check, because it is a valid number, and it is a thousand times smaller than the amount in the file.

The column votes again, and this time the candidates are pairs of marks, one that groups thousands and one that starts the decimals. Dot and comma is one pair, comma and dot another, space and comma a third. A pair reads a value only when the digit groups sit where that pair expects them, so 1.234,56 fits dot and comma and fails comma and dot. Before the vote, the importer strips the currency symbol, normalizes the non-breaking space, and turns (250,00) into -250.

The column settles values that look identical on their own. 1,234 means 1234 in a column that also holds 1,234.56, and 1.234 in a column that also holds 1.234,56. A column of nothing but 1,234 ties the way dates do.

Value mapping works on distinct values

Some fields accept only a fixed list of values, such as a department, a status, or a country. People type those values in their own words, with different spelling, case, and abbreviations. The importer turns every variant into one of the values the app accepts.

The file's Department column already matched the department field by its header, and a lookup table converts the words.

const DEPARTMENTS = { Engineering: "eng", Sales: "sales" };
row.department = DEPARTMENTS[row.department];

The column holds Engineering, engineering, Eng, R&D, and Enginering. The table finds the first and returns undefined for the other four. The header matched, and the values inside the column still use the words of whoever typed them.

The importer collects the unique values of the column, resolves each one once, and applies the finished mapping to every row as a lookup. A million rows with five spellings of a department need five decisions. Fuzzy string matching that ignores case pairs engineering and Enginering with Engineering.

String similarity alone does not tell you that R&D means Engineering, or that Eng is short for it. That knowledge belongs to your domain. It reaches the mapping through a synonym list you keep, through your own logic, such as the mappings the same customer confirmed last time, or through the person importing the file, who picks the value by hand.

The browser decodes every file as UTF-8

A file on disk is a sequence of bytes, and an encoding is the rule that turns those bytes into letters. Older systems and different countries use different rules. When the app reads a file with the wrong rule, letters such as ü and é come out broken.

The import code at the start of this article reads the file with file.text(), which always decodes it as UTF-8. A CSV written by an older system in Windows-1252 stores ü as the single byte FC, which is invalid in UTF-8. The decoder swaps it for a replacement character, and Müller arrives as M�ller. The opposite mistake, UTF-8 bytes read as Windows-1252, turns Müller into MÃ¼ller.

The replacement character is final. Once � sits in the string, nothing recovers the letter it replaced, so the decision has to happen while the bytes are still in hand. The importer checks for a byte order mark first, because it can identify several Unicode encodings before any guessing is needed. Then it tries UTF-8 in strict mode, where an invalid byte makes the decoder throw.

const decoder = new TextDecoder("utf-8", { fatal: true });
const text = decoder.decode(await file.arrayBuffer());

If strict decoding throws, the bytes are not valid UTF-8. Only then does the importer infer a legacy encoding from the bytes with a detector such as chardet, and decode again with the label it returns.

Large files break both parsing and rendering

Every fix so far works on a file of a few hundred rows. A file with a million rows asks the browser to read, process, and show all of it while the page stays responsive.

The import code at the start of this article runs on the main thread, which also paints the page and answers clicks. As the importer gains decoding, parsing, format detection, and value mapping, doing that work on the main thread turns it into one long task, and the tab stops responding until it ends.

The importer hands the File object to a Web Worker and decodes and parses there, so the page keeps painting. Some cost stays on the main thread. On 4 September 2026 I ran a 108 MB CSV with one million rows and eleven columns through a worker in Chrome 151. The main thread stayed free while the worker parsed, and still hit one 389 ms task when the parsed rows arrived back. A worker that reads the file in one call also holds the whole file in memory.

The rows then reach the second limit. A normal DOM table does not scale to a million rows, because every cell it renders is an element the browser lays out and paints. The grid has to limit rendering to a small window around the visible rows and work out the rest from the scroll position. A virtualized list does that with elements, and a canvas grid does it with pixels.

An importer answers what the data means

Other files break a simple CSV import in other ways. A report can place its header row several lines down, under a title and a blank line. Two columns can share the header id, and PapaParse renames the second to id_1, which no field in the app expects. A short row can shift its values into the wrong columns. An Excel workbook can hold several sheets, and only one of them holds the data.

A CSV parser answers whether a file can be read. An importer has to answer what the data means, what is wrong with it, what the person can fix, and what the app should receive.

I learned most of this while building Updog, a client-side importer for CSV and Excel files.

I wrote this article with the help of AI.

articles.title: Building an Auth Backend: JWT, Refresh Tokens, Rate Limiting, and Timing Attacks Explained
articles.description: Every backend I start ends up with the same handful of pieces: access and refresh tokens, a rate...
articles.body_html:
Every backend I start ends up with the same handful of pieces: access and refresh tokens, a rate limiter that survives concurrent requests instead of quietly losing count, a login route that doesn't leak information through response time, and one consistent response shape across every route. None of it is exotic. But explaining why each piece is shaped the way it is always took longer than writing the code itself — so instead of writing another wall of text, I built a page that walks through it.

Live demo: auth-architecture-explorer-demo
Repo: auth-architecture-explorer-repo

It's six sections, each one a small interactive piece of the backend, laid out like blueprint sheets.

The request pipeline

Nothing hits a route handler directly. Every request falls through eight middleware layers first, in a fixed order — and the order matters, though it's worth being honest about where it comes from. Some of it is a real design decision: the rate limiter sits above the routers specifically so abuse never reaches a database-heavy handler, and that choice is deliberate. Some of it is closer to convention — Express's typical middleware chain nudges people toward this order by default, and an equally valid alternative exists (auth first, with public routes like /auth/login explicitly whitelisted instead of relying on ordering). I'm not presenting this pipeline as the correct order, just as one coherent choice with a clear reason behind the parts that are load-bearing.

The explainer animates a signal down a vertical trace, lighting up each stage as a real request would pass through it — express.json(), then helmet(), then cors(), and so on down to the router. Watching it step through in order made one thing obvious that reading the list never quite does: the rate limiter runs before authentication middleware, which means req.user is usually still undefined at that point. That's not a bug — it's protecting unauthenticated routes like /auth/login too — but it's the kind of detail that's easy to explain wrong if you haven't actually traced it.

Two tokens, doing two different jobs

An access token is a JWT — short-lived, verified by signature alone, no database hit on every request. A refresh token is the opposite on purpose: long-lived, opaque, tracked in a database row, checked against a stored hash every time it's used.

The split exists because a stateless token can never be revoked early. So the one thing that actually needs to be revocable — the refresh token — is the one thing that's tracked, and the thing that gets used on every single request stays cheap and stateless.

In the demo, logging in shows both tokens animate in, then the access token's fields quietly count down while the refresh token's stay fixed — a small, literal way of showing that these two things are trusted for completely different lengths of time.

Worth flagging up front, since it bears on the next section too: this refresh token doesn't rotate on use, so there's no built-in way to detect if a copy of it leaked. More on that in the limitations section — it's not an oversight, but it is a real gap, not just a footnote.

Why a naive rate limiter loses requests

This is the section I'd point to first if someone asked what the whole page was for.

Two requests from the same user can land in the same millisecond. If your rate limiter reads the current count, increments it in application code, and writes it back — both requests can read the same starting value, both increment from it, and one increment just disappears. No error, no crash. The count is wrong and nothing tells you.

sql
INSERT INTO rate_limits (user_id, count, window_start)
VALUES ($user, 1, now())
ON CONFLICT (user_id) DO UPDATE SET
  count = CASE WHEN window_start < now() - windowSeconds
          THEN 1 ELSE count + 1 END,
  window_start = CASE WHEN window_start < now() - windowSeconds
          THEN now() ELSE window_start END

The fix is a single atomic

INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE

— Postgres serializes the write at the row level instead of the coordination happening (or not happening) in your own code. The demo runs both versions side by side: the naive one visibly drops a request, the atomic one doesn't, and there's a small measured line showing how often the naive version actually loses count under overlap.

One caveat I want to be upfront about: that measured number comes from a simulation running in the browser, not from an actual Postgres instance under load. It's a faithful illustration of the race itself — two concurrent reads racing a shared counter — but it doesn't reproduce real-world factors like lock contention, connection pooling, or network latency. So treat the demo as proof that the failure mode exists and that the atomic fix closes it, not as a benchmark of how often this happens in production. If you want that number, you'd need to run the actual queries against a real database under concurrent load — the repo doesn't do that (yet).

The timing leak in a login route that looks fine

A login endpoint that returns immediately when a username doesn't exist is fast. One that runs a full password comparison is slow. If both return the identical error message, that seems safe — until you notice the response time is different, and an attacker doesn't need to read your error message to learn something from that.

// looks harmless, leaks timing
const user = await db.findUser(email);
if (!user) return { error: "Invalid credentials" }; // fast, no hashing ran
const valid = await bcrypt.compare(password, user.hash); // slow

The fix is running the same slow comparison unconditionally — against a precomputed dummy hash when there's no real user to check against — so the response takes the same time either way. The demo has a toggle between the two versions and two bars that are dramatically different lengths in "quick exit" mode and identical once "always compare" is on.

To be clear about scope: this fix closes the leak on the login route specifically. Any other endpoint that branches on "does this record exist" before doing expensive work — password reset requests, email-availability checks during signup, invite-code validation — can leak the same way through the same mechanism, and needs the same fix applied separately. Fixing login alone doesn't fix the pattern everywhere it appears.

What I'd actually change at scale

I didn't want this to read like everything here is a finished, ideal system, because it isn't. Three honest limitations, stated plainly on the last real section before the footer:

The IP-based limiter is in-memory, so it wouldn't stay in sync across multiple server instances — a shared store would fix that.
The refresh token doesn't rotate, so there's no automatic reuse detection if a copy leaks — only a manual logout revokes it early.
The access token is never cross-checked against the database, so there's a short window after logout where an already-issued one still works.

None of these are oversights I didn't notice — they're trade-offs I made on purpose, mostly toward simplicity, and I'd rather say so directly than let the interactive demo imply more confidence than the system actually has.

Why build the explainer instead of just writing the README

I could describe an atomic upsert in text and trust that "two requests reading the same stale value" lands. But watching two requests race against a naive counter, seeing the increment vanish, then watching the same race resolve correctly against the atomic version — that's a different kind of understanding than reading a paragraph about it. I wanted the failure to be visible, not just described — with the caveat, stated plainly above, that "visible" here means a browser simulation of the mechanism, not a production-scale measurement.

It's built with React, no backend of its own — every interaction on the page is a client-side simulation, including the "measured" numbers, which come from a small real simulation run in the browser rather than a hardcoded guess.

Repo's public if you want to see how any of the sections are put together, or reuse the pattern for your own backend's docs. If you've made different calls on any of this — rotating refresh tokens, session-based auth instead of JWT, a different rate-limiting store — I'd genuinely like to hear the reasoning.
